title: "Go, you are free"
hookLine: he forgives the people who drove him out, echoing Yusuf, no blame on you today (12:92)

lines: THE PEOPLE WHO DROVE HIM OUT.
WHAT DO YOU THINK I'LL DO?
cards: The square around the Ka'ba is full that day, and the faces are familiar. Some of these people mocked him in the street for years.

Some boycotted his clan, shutting them up hungry in a narrow valley, chased him out of his hometown, and fought him at Badr and Uhud. One woman in that crowd had rejoiced over the body of his uncle Hamzah.

Now the city is his, and no army is left to stop him. The early biographies say he asked them: what do you think I'm going to do to you? They answered carefully, the way you answer when your life depends on it: good.
You're a noble brother, the son of a noble brother.

teach.h: WHAT YUSUF SAID TO HIS BROTHERS.
teach.b: According to the early accounts of his life, he said: I say to you what Yusuf said to his brothers.
No blame on you today. Go, you are free. He didn't make up a speech.
He reached for a story everyone listening knew. In the Qur'an's twelfth surah, Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away.
Years later they stand before him in Egypt, hungry, not knowing who he is, and when they finally realize, they're ashamed.

And Yusuf says, in the Qur'an's words, that there is no blame on them this day, and that God will forgive them. The Prophet stepped into that story on purpose: you're my brothers, and I'm doing what Yusuf did.
The reports call the people of Mecca after this the tulaqa', the freed ones. Notice what this forgiveness is not.
It isn't pretending nothing happened; everyone in that square knew exactly what had happened, and that's why they were afraid. It isn't weakness either; he could have done anything.

It's choosing, from strength, not to collect the debt. Some of the people let go that day became Muslims, and some later became leaders of the community. Muslim teachers often point out that some were his own relatives.
Family is often the hardest place to say: go, you're free.

how: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca as a model of mercy, and many teachers use it, together with Yusuf's words to his brothers, when urging people to forgive relatives and old enemies.

o: the signal for his army to march on the city
an order to leave Mecca and never come back home
his first word in pardoning those who drove him out

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: no blame on you, to his brothers

s: the Prophet ﷺ made up new words for the moment
he said he was saying what Yusuf said to his brothers, from surah 12.
some of the people he forgave were his own relatives
the Quraysh of Mecca were his own tribe and family.
some of the people let go that day later became Muslims
and some later became leaders of the community.

games.q: you're the Prophet ﷺ. the city that drove you out is yours, and the people who fought you stand waiting. what do you do?
o: punish the leaders as a warning.
say what Yusuf said: no blame on you today. go, you are free.
leave the city to them and go home to Medina.
games.why: the early biographies say he quoted Yusuf and let them go. the people of Mecca were called the tulaqa', the freed ones.

practice: Think of someone who hurt you long ago: not the worst thing that ever happened to you, just something you've carried a while.

You don't have to call them or say it was fine; just picture them and see if you can let the debt go, even a little. If you pray, you can ask God to forgive them, and you; if you don't, just try the words quietly: go, you're free.

wordCard.voice: Go. The first word of what he told the people who'd driven him out: go, you are free. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the freed ones, the name given to the people of Mecca let go that day.

carryVoice: Your line: no blame on you today. Yusuf said it first. Day two hundred seventy-eight, done.

sources.ref: Qur'an 12:92 (Yusuf to his brothers: no blame on you this day; God will forgive you)
